issues.explanation: The trigger set is not coherent with the trauma type and the rest of the profile. For terrorism trauma in a prosecutor, 'Happy families' could plausibly trigger loss/safety themes, but 'Medical equipment such as needles or drips' points toward a medical trauma context that is not otherwise represented in the memory or appraisal items. This looks like a hard-to-explain trigger mismatch rather than ordinary heterogeneity.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: 'I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is typically associated with interpersonal/sexual trauma or moral contamination themes. In this profile, the other appraisals are inaction guilt and distrust, and the memory items describe vivid, present-tense traumatic reliving of a terrorism event. Without any sexual assault, bodily violation, or contamination-related trigger/memory content, this appraisal is clinically discordant with the trauma type and the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: For a terrorism trauma in a 33-year-old prosecutor, the selected trigger set is weakly anchored to the trauma described. 'Needles/medical equipment' could occur if he sustained injuries, and 'alcohol smell' could occur if alcohol was present during aftermath or coping, but together they imply a medical/assault-like or hospital-associated cue pattern that is not supported anywhere else in the profile. With no memory or appraisal content linking the trauma to injury treatment, intoxication, or bodily violation, these triggers are clinically hard to place.

'I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is more typical of sexual assault, moral contamination, or exposure involving bodily fluids. In a terrorism case it is not impossible, but here it is not supported by the rest of the selected items: the memories emphasize disorganization and nowness, and the appraisals emphasize guilt and distrust, not bodily violation or pollution. This makes the contamination item the least coherent appraisal in the set.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: For an adult male prosecutor with terrorism trauma, the appraisal of feeling 'dirty or contaminated' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other items center on sensory trauma triggers (alcohol smell, explosion sounds), disorganized yet vivid reliving memory, and guilt/distrust appraisals, which fit terrorism exposure. 'Contamination' more strongly suggests trauma involving sexual assault, bodily violation, or moral taint, and here it lacks support from the memory, trigger, or strategy nodes. This makes it a clinically questionable outlier within the allowed components.

vignette: Caleb Vance stood near the marble entrance of the federal courthouse annex, his briefcase heavy with witness affidavits, when the world simply detonated. He had never imagined a car bomb in his own city, but the vehicle idling near the security checkpoint had been rigged. The initial blast threw him against a concrete pillar, followed by a secondary explosion that shattered the glass facade and sent shrapnel across the plaza. Through the ringing silence that followed, Caleb scrambled to his feet, coughing through a haze of smoke. He saw colleagues trapped under debris, heard their cries, and felt an overwhelming urge to rush toward them, but his own legs would not obey. The smoke carried a sharp scent of spilled whiskey and gasoline. He watched a fellow assistant district attorney slump over a shattered display case, and despite his training, he could only stand frozen until emergency responders pulled him backward. The event was never a clean sequence of cause and effect; it remained a fractured tableau that never truly closed. In the months that followed, the fragmentation of that afternoon dictated his reality. Caleb found he could not tell a clear story of what happened even to himself, and the lack of a coherent story only deepened his disorientation. When the alcohol smell hit him at a firm networking dinner, his breath would catch, his pulse would spike, and that olfactory cue directly fueled his inaction guilt and his conviction that he had failed to protect those who needed him most. The sensory trigger did not merely startle him; it actively cemented his belief that he could not trust the safety of ordinary spaces, driving him to distrust others and assume their reassurances were masks for the same helplessness he had felt. Because he carried the unshakable conviction that he had failed and that the world was fundamentally unsafe, the traumatic memories only grew more immediate and intrusive. He would sit at his desk in his windowless conference room, the paperweights and legal pads around him blurring, until the memory felt present not past, the heat of the fire and the weight of the dust pressing against his skin. These recollections were vivid and tactile, so much more real than normal that they bypassed his professional composure entirely. The way they returned, unbidden and suffocating, constantly reinforced his self-reproach and paranoia. Every time the traumatic scene played out in his mind, fresh and unedited, it validated his belief that he had failed to protect others and that his inaction was unforgivable, directly feeding back into the very appraisals that kept him trapped. As those memories surged with such visceral force, they sharpened his threat monitoring until even a passing fatigue from late brief-writing became a warning signal. When he began feeling very tired or exhausted after long court days, his mind would catastrophize, interpreting physical depletion as the body’s first sign of collapse. That exhaustion then made him hyperalert to any sudden bang from the courtroom gallery or the street below. The auditory cue of an explosion or bang sound would immediately hijack his nervous system, proving that his fragmented recall was not just a psychological echo, but a physiological trigger that kept him braced for a secondary blast. The avoidance habits that formed over the subsequent year slowly dismantled his professional life. He started avoiding evening court sessions, taking early departures, and skipping social gatherings where drinks were poured. His senior partners noticed his withdrawn demeanor and declining trial readiness, while his wife, Elena, worried over the man who flinched when she set down her wine glass. The breaking point came when Caleb misfiled a critical motion because he had fallen asleep at his kitchen table, exhausted from yet another night spent bracing for a catastrophe that never came. He realized his attempts to stay hyper-vigilant were dismantling the very case he had built his career on, and his marriage was fraying under the weight of his silence. He finally scheduled an intake, hoping for relief from the suffocating cycle, though his greatest fear remained that help would not be enough to quiet the memories or rewrite the guilt that had taken root. He wanted to stop flinching at the sound of slamming doors and to look at his wife without wondering what he had missed, what he could have done differently, and whether he could ever trust the quiet again.
